Exhortation to Repentance; Judgment on Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah.</title> <div sID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> Belonging to an earlier period than the twenty-first chapter, namely, the reigns of Shallum or Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.10">Jr 22:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.20">13, 20</reference>). Jeremiah often groups his prophecies, not by chronological order, but by similarity of subjects; thus <reference osisRef="Jer.22.3">Jr 22:3</reference> corresponds to <reference osisRef="Jer.21.12">Jr 21:12</reference>. Grotius thinks that Jeremiah here repeats to Zedekiah what he had announced to that king's predecessors formerly (namely, his brother and brother's son), of a similar bearing, and which had since come to pass; a warning to Zedekiah. Probably, in arranging his prophecies they were grouped for the first time in the present order, designed by the Holy Spirit to set forth the series of kings of Judah, all four alike, failing in "righteousness," followed at last by the "King," a righteous Branch raised unto David, in the house of Judah, "the Lord our righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>). The unrighteousness of Zedekiah suggested the review of his predecessors' failure in the same respects, and consequent punishment, which ought to have warned him, but did not.<div eID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10051"/><hi type="bold">1. Go down--</hi>The temple (where Jeremiah had been prophesying) was higher than the king's palace on Mount Zion (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.10">Jr 36:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.36.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.23.20">2Ch 23:20</reference>). Hence the phrase, "Go down."<div eID="gen17914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the king of Judah--</hi>perhaps including each of the four successive kings, to whom it was consecutively addressed, here brought together in one picture: Shallum, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.11">Jr 22:11</reference>; Jehoiakim, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13-Jer.22.18">Jr 22:13-18</reference>; Jeconiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>; Zedekiah, the address to whom (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.1">Jr 21:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.12">11, 12</reference>) suggests notice of the rest. <div eID="gen17915" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 22 Jr 22:1-30 . Exhortation to Repentance; Judgment on Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah. Belonging to an earlier period than the twenty-first chapter, namely, the reigns of Shallum or Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Jeconiah ( Jr 22:10 , 13, 20 ). Jeremiah often groups his prophecies, not by chronological order, but by similarity of subjects; thus Jr 22:3 corresponds to Jr 21:12 . Grotius thinks that Jeremiah here repeats to Zedekiah what he had announced to that king's predecessors formerly (namely, his brother and brother's son), of a similar bearing, and which had since come to pass; a warning to Zedekiah. Probably, in arranging his prophecies they were grouped for the first time in the present order, designed by the Holy Spirit to set forth the series of kings of Judah, all four alike, failing in "righteousness," followed at last by the "King," a righteous Branch raised unto David, in the house of Judah, "the Lord our righteousness" ( Jr 23:6 ). The unrighteousness of Zedekiah suggested the review of his predecessors' failure in the same respects, and consequent punishment, which ought to have warned him, but did not. 1. Go down-- The temple (where Jeremiah had been prophesying) was higher than the king's palace on Mount Zion ( Jr 36:10 , 12 ; 2Ch 23:20 ). Hence the phrase, "Go down." the king of Judah-- perhaps including each of the four successive kings, to whom it was consecutively addressed, here brought together in one picture: Shallum, Jr 22:11 ; Jehoiakim, Jr 22:13-18 ; Jeconiah, Jr 22:24 ; Zedekiah, the address to whom ( Jr 21:1 , 11, 12 ) suggests notice of the rest.

Though thou art as beautiful as Gilead, and as majestic in Mine eyes (before Me) as the summit of Lebanon, yet surely (the Hebrew is a formula of swearing to express certainly: "If I do not make thee ... believe Me not ever hereafter": so "as truly as I live," <reference osisRef="Num.14.28">Nu 14:28</reference>; "surely," <reference osisRef="Num.14.35">Nu 14:35</reference>). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10060"/><div sID="gen17928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10060"/><hi type="bold">10-11. Weep ... not for--</hi>that is, not so much for Josiah, who was taken away by death from the evil to come (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.22.20">2Ki 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Is 57:1</reference>); as for Shallum or Jehoahaz, his son (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.30">2Ki 23:30</reference>), who, after a three months' reign, was carried off by Pharaoh-necho into Egypt, never to see his native land again (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31-2Kgs.23.34">2Ki 23:31-34</reference>). Dying saints are justly to be envied, while living sinners are to be pitied. The allusion is to the great weeping of the people at the death of Josiah, and on each anniversary of it, in which Jeremiah himself took a prominent part (<reference osisRef="2Chr.35.24">2Ch 35:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">25</reference>). The name "Shallum" is here given in irony to Jehoahaz, who reigned but three months; as if he were a second Shallum, son of Jabesh, who reigned only one month in Samaria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.13">2Ki 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1-2Chr.36.4">2Ch 36:1-4</reference>). Shallum means "retribution," a name of no good omen to him [Grotius]; originally the people called him Shallom, indicative of peace and prosperity. But Jeremiah applies it in irony. <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.15">1Ch 3:15</reference>, calls Shallum the fourth son of Josiah. The people raised him to the throne before his brother Eliakim or Jehoiakim, though the latter was the older (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31">2Ki 23:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.36">36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.1">2Ch 36:1</reference>); perhaps on account of Jehoiakim's extravagance (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15">15</reference>). Jehoiakim was put in Shallum's (Jehoahaz') stead by Pharaoh-necho. Jeconiah, his son, succeeded. Zedekiah (Mattaniah), uncle of Jeconiah, and brother of Jehoiakim and Jehoahaz, was last of all raised to the throne by Nebuchadnezzar.<div eID="gen17928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17929" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">He shall not return--</hi>The people perhaps entertained hopes of Shallum's return from Egypt, in which case they would replace him on the throne, and thereby free themselves from the oppressive taxes imposed by Jehoiakim. <div eID="gen17929" type="x-p"/>

He shall not return-- The people perhaps entertained hopes of Shallum's return from Egypt, in which case they would replace him on the throne, and thereby free themselves from the oppressive taxes imposed by Jehoiakim.

Not only did Jehoiakim tax the people (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.35">2Ki 23:35</reference>) for Pharaoh's tribute, but also took their forced labor, without pay, for building a splendid palace; in violation of <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Le 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.24.14">De 24:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">15</reference>. Upper rooms in the East are the principal apartments.<div eID="gen17932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17933" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cutteth him out windows--</hi>The Hebrew, if a noun, is rather, "my windows"; then the translation ought to be, "and let my windows (Jehoiakim speaking) be cut out for it," that is, in the house; or, "and let (the workman) cut out my windows for it." But the word is rather an adjective; "he cutteth it (the house) out for himself, so as to be full of windows." entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10066"/><div sID="gen17940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10066"/><hi type="bold">18. Ah my brother! ... sister!--</hi>addressing him with such titles of affection as one would address to a deceased friend beloved as a brother or sister (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.30">1Ki 13:30</reference>). This expresses, They shall not lament him with the lamentation of private individuals [Vatablus], or of blood relatives [Grotius]: as "Ah! lord," expresses public lamentation in the case of a king [Vatablus], or that of subjects [Grotius]. Henderson thinks, "Ah! sister," refers to Jehoiakim's queen, who, though taken to Babylon and not left unburied on the way, as Jehoiakim, yet was not honored at her death with royal lamentations, such as would have been poured forth over her at Jerusalem. He notices the beauty of Jeremiah's manner in his prophecy against Jehoiakim. In <reference osisRef="Jer.22.13">Jr 22:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.14">14</reference> he describes him in general terms; then, in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.17">Jr 22:15-17</reference>, he directly addresses him without naming him; at last, in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.18">Jr 22:18</reference>, he names him, but in the third person, to imply that God puts him to a distance from Him. The boldness of the Hebrew prophets proves their divine mission; were it not so, their reproofs to the Hebrew kings, who held the throne by divine authority, would have been treason.<div eID="gen17940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ah his glory!--</hi>"Alas! his majesty." <div eID="gen17941" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10067"/><div sID="gen17942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10067"/><hi type="bold">19. burial of an ass--</hi>that is, he shall have the same burial as an ass would get, namely, he shall be left a prey for beasts and birds [Jerome]. This is not formally narrated. But <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.6">2Ch 36:6</reference> states that "Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon"; his treatment there is nowhere mentioned. The prophecy here, and in <reference osisRef="Jer.36.30">Jr 36:30</reference>, harmonizes these two facts. He was slain by Nebuchadnezzar, who changed his purpose of taking him to Babylon, on the way thither, and left him unburied outside Jerusalem. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.6">2Ki 24:6</reference>, "Jehoiakim slept with his fathers," does not contradict this; it simply expresses his being gathered to his fathers by death, not his being buried with his fathers (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">Psa 49:19</reference>). The two phrases are found together, as expressing two distinct ideas (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.38">2Ki 15:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.20">16:20</reference>). <div eID="gen17942" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10068"/><div sID="gen17943" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10068"/>20. The passes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.4">1Sa 14:4</reference>).
